How much does connectivity matter when composition is unchanged? Compare a
linear chain with a comb made from exactly the same Gaussian blocks. In the
comb, three side chains branch from backbone junctions; there is no spherical
core or distributed surface attachment.

This tutorial assumes the [diblock workflow](diblock-copolymer.qmd). Lengths
are in nm and q is in inverse nm.

## Build two topologies from the same blocks

The backbone contains four blocks and the side chains contain three. Shared
`backbone` and `side` tags give each family its own physical parameters.
Branching at a common endpoint is a fixed junction: it is different from
attaching a chain to a randomly sampled position along a polymer contour.

```text
comb:    b1 -- b2 -- b3 -- b4
              |     |     |
              s1    s2    s3

linear:  b1 -- b2 -- b3 -- b4 -- s1 -- s2 -- s3
```

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pyseb


def build_model(topology):
    world = pyseb.World(f"{topology}Tutorial")
    graph = world.Add("GaussianPolymer", "b1", "backbone")
    for index in range(2, 5):
        world.Link("GaussianPolymer", f"b{index}.end1",
                   f"b{index - 1}.end2", "backbone")
    for index in range(1, 4):
        if topology == "comb":
            target = f"b{index}.end2"
        else:
            target = "b4.end2" if index == 1 else f"s{index - 1}.end2"
        world.Link("GaussianPolymer", f"s{index}.end1", target, "side")
    world.Add(graph, "molecule")
    return world


comb = build_model("comb")
linear = build_model("linear")
parameters = {
    "beta_backbone": 1.0,
    "Rg_backbone": 2.0,
    "beta_side": 0.8,
    "Rg_side": 3.0,
}
```

Every `Link` adds a new subunit. The result is a tree with no closed cycles.
The two worlds use identical parameter dictionaries and total scattering
lengths; only the links differ.

## Compare size and form factor

```{python}
q = np.geomspace(1e-3, 2.0, 180)
for label, world in (("comb", comb), ("linear", linear)):
    rg2 = world.EvaluateRadiusOfGyration2("molecule", parameters)
    curve = np.asarray(world.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", parameters, q.tolist()))
    assert np.all(np.isfinite(curve))
    assert np.isclose(world.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", parameters, 0.0), 1.0)
    print(f"{label}: Rg = {np.sqrt(rg2):.4f} nm")
    plt.loglog(q, curve, label=label)
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ (nm$^{-1}$)")
plt.ylabel(r"$F(q)$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

Both normalized curves approach one at small q. Branching shortens paths
between blocks, making this comb more compact than the linear arrangement.
The different radii of gyration therefore already distinguish the topologies
in the Guinier region. Unlike the [rod–coil comparison](rod-coil.qmd), we hold
composition and individual block dimensions fixed rather than matching total
size.

```{python}
_ = pyseb.visualize(comb, "molecule", parameters, height=440, layouts=["random", "readable"])
_ = pyseb.visualize(linear, "molecule", parameters, height=440, layouts=["random", "readable"])
```

The drawings are representative random walks. Crossings do not create links,
and these ideal Gaussian blocks do not include excluded-volume interactions.

## Hide the side chains by contrast matching

Setting `beta_side` to zero removes side-chain scattering without removing
the branches from the topology. Because both models have the same backbone,
the resulting form factors coincide. This is a useful check that the original
difference involves the side chains and their correlations with other blocks.

```{python}
matched = dict(parameters, beta_side=0.0)
comb_matched = np.asarray(comb.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", matched, q.tolist()))
linear_matched = np.asarray(linear.EvaluateFormFactor("molecule", matched, q.tolist()))
assert np.allclose(comb_matched, linear_matched)
plt.loglog(q, comb_matched, label="comb, side chains matched")
plt.loglog(q, linear_matched, "--", label="linear, side blocks matched")
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ (nm$^{-1}$)")
plt.ylabel(r"$F(q)$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

Try changing `Rg_side` with both families visible. Then vary the side-chain
scattering weight separately. Changing a dimension and changing contrast
answer different questions, even though either can change the measured curve.
